ref: Against Beron and Helix, Fragment V (ANF 5 Dogmatical part; Migne PG 10 cols ~[1754]-[1756])
greek: Βήρων γάρ τις ἔναγχος μεθ᾽ ἑτέρων τινῶν τὴν Βαλεντίνου φαντασίαν ἀφέντες, χείρονι κακῷ κατεπάρησαν, λέγοντες τὴν μὲν προσληφθεῖσαν τῷ Λόγῳ σάρκα γενέσθαι ταύτουργον τῇ θεότητι διὰ τὴν πρόσληψιν, τὴν θεότητα δὲ γενέσθαι ταὐτοπαθῆ τῇ σαρκὶ διὰ κένωσιν ... εἰ δὲ φύσεων αὐτοῖς συγκεχυμένων ἔσται δυὰς ὁ Χριστός, καὶ προσώπων μεμερισμένων τετράς, τὸ φευκτότατον.
greek_edition: Lagarde 1858 (Teubner), archive.org hippolytiromani00lagagoog, text-layer PDF dl/lagarde1858_text_layer.pdf; OCR (not visually checked) p. 61-62 (PDF p. 82, header '61'); OCR noise (ταύτουργον, accents) kept as read; marginal numbers removed
english: "...if the natures are fused together, Christ will be a duality; and if the persons are separated, there will be a quaternity, a thing which is altogether to be avoided." The ANF gloss reads: "tetras, i.e., instead of Trinity [the Trias]."
page: Lagarde 1858 p. 61-62; ANF 5 page unknown (ANF bracket cols [1753]-[1756])
what_it_says: Hippolytus' opponents' Christology is attacked because separating persons would yield a 'quaternity' rather than a Trinity; the Greek word for Trinity (triás) does not appear in the fragment.
limits: The word 'Trinity' is the translator's gloss, not Hippolytus' Greek. The fragment argues against Christological error (Beron), not for a developed Trinitarian doctrine.

ref: Against Beron and Helix, Fragment IV (ANF 5; bracket cols [1744]-[1747])
greek: Τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον τῆς θείως σαρκώσεως ἀποστόλοις τε καὶ προφήταις καὶ διδασκάλοις διττὴν καὶ διάφορον ἔχον διέγνωσται τὴν ἐν πᾶσι φυσικὴν θεωρίαν ... ἕως ἂν εἷς κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν γνωρίζεται λόγος μιᾶς ἐνεργείας, οὐδέποτε καθ᾽ ὁτιοῦν ἀμφοτέρων γνωσθήσεται κίνησιν.
greek_edition: Lagarde 1858 (Teubner), archive.org hippolytiromani00lagagoog, text-layer PDF dl/lagarde1858_text_layer.pdf; OCR (not visually checked) p. 61 (PDF p. 82); OCR variants noted: 'οὐχ.' read for ἂν, 'Χίνησι' for κίνησιν; accents as read
english: "As long, therefore, as the Word is acknowledged to be in substance one, of one energy, there shall never in any way be known a movement in the two."
what_it_says: In the Incarnation the Word is one in substance and of one energy, so the divine and human are not confused.
limits: A Christological statement (one Word in the Incarnation), not a statement about the three persons; 'in substance' is used of the Word only.

ref: Discourse on the Holy Theophany (the ANF title; the 'Homily on the Holy Pascha' of the brief is not this text by ANF's title) ch. 8, ANF bracket [1822]-[1823]
greek: Ὁ τῆς ἀθανασίας Πατὴρ, τὸν ἀθάνατον Υἱὸν καὶ Λόγον ἀπέστειλεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον· ὃς ἀφικόμενος εἰς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, λούσασθαι ὕδατι καὶ Πνεύματι· καὶ ἀναγεννήσας πρὸς ἀφθαρσίαν ψυχῆς τε καὶ σώματος, ἐνεφύσησεν ἡμῖν πνεῦμα ζωῆς
greek_edition: Migne PG 10 (1857), archive.org patrologiaecursu10mignuoft, djvu OCR; Greek OCR, not visually checked; PDF 79 MB, not downloaded; column per ANF bracket numbering, not checked against the printed column
english: "The Father of immortality sent the immortal Son and Word into the world, who came to man in order to wash him with water and the Spirit; and He, begetting us again to incorruption of soul and body, breathed into us the breath (spirit) of life..."
page: page unknown (PG 10 column per ANF bracket)
what_it_says: Baptism is described as the Father sending the Son and Word, with water and the Holy Spirit as the means of regeneration.
limits: It names Father, Son, Word and Spirit together in one baptismal economy, but gives no formula of co-equality or consubstantiality. Authorship of this discourse is not verified in the sources read.

ref: Discourse on the Holy Theophany, end doxology (ANF 5 ch. 10; bracket [1837]-[1838])
greek: Αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος σὺν τῷ παναγίῳ καὶ ἀγαθῷ καὶ ζωοποιῷ αὐτοῦ Πνεύματι, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ
greek_edition: Migne PG 10 (1857), archive.org patrologiaecursu10mignuoft, djvu OCR; Greek OCR, not visually checked; PDF 79 MB, not downloaded; OCR read cleanly here
english: "To Him be the glory and the power, together with His most holy, and good, and quickening Spirit, now and ever..."
what_it_says: A doxology ascribes glory and power to an unnamed 'Him' together with the Holy Spirit.
limits: 'Him' is not named (the Son, or the Father, per context); the doxology is not an explicit Trinitarian formula. Shares the ambiguity common to early doxologies.

ref: Doubtful Fragments on the Pentateuch, Preface (ANF 5 Exegetical part; ANF bracket [1363])
greek_edition: No Greek located in the Lagarde/PG 10 OCR searches; ANF text states the law was given 'in the Syriac tongue of the Targum' (translated from Syriac)
english: "In the name of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God. This is a transcript of the excellent law."
what_it_says: The text opens with a baptismal-style Trinitarian formula ('one God') and then presents a chronicle of the law's transmission.
limits: Under ANF's heading 'Doubtful Fragments'; a Syriac-tradition text. It cannot be cited as Hippolytus' own Greek; its formula is not dated to Hippolytus.

ref: Canons of the Church of Alexandria, Canon I (ANF 5 Appendix; heading 'Wrongly ascribed to Hippolytus', bracket [2075]-[2076])
greek_edition: No Greek read; ANF text in English only
english: "...the Trinity is equal perfectly in honour, and equal in glory, and has neither beginning nor end. The Word is the Son of God, and is Himself the Creator of every creature..."
translator: not read in the ANF text (ANF appendix translator not confirmed)
what_it_says: A canon text (ANF: wrongly ascribed to Hippolytus) affirms equal honour and glory of the Trinity, eternal, with the Word as Creator.
limits: Not Hippolytus; late canon collection. Cited only to show that Trinitarian language appears in pseudepigrapha, not in his genuine works.

ref: Pseudo-Hippolytus, Discourse on the End of the World and Antichrist (ANF 5 Appendix, 'Containing Dubious and Spurious Pieces'), ch. 29, bracket [2004]
greek_edition: Greek not located in PG 10 OCR searches; not quoted
english: "Thou art the ever-living One. Thou art without beginning, like the Father, and co-eternal with the Spirit."
what_it_says: In an address to Christ at judgment, the speaker calls Him without beginning like the Father and co-eternal with the Spirit.
limits: Spurious/dubious (ANF heading). Greek not checked; a late text, so it is not evidence for Hippolytus' own theology.

ref: Hippolytus, Fragment IV, 'Discourse on Elkanah and Hannah' (ANF 5 Dogmatical part; 'In Theodoret, Dial. I'; bracket [1851])
greek: Ἄγε δή μοι, ὦ Σαμουήλ, εἰς Βηθλεὲμ ἑλκομένην τὴν δάμαλιν, ἵνα ἐπιδείξῃς τὸν ἐκ Δαβὶδ βασιλέα τικτόμενον... λόγος γὰρ θεοῦ πρωτότοκος ἐξ οὐρανῶν ἐπὶ τὴν μακαρίαν Μαρίαν κατερχόμενος
greek_edition: Lagarde 1858 (Teubner), archive.org hippolytiromani00lagagoog, text-layer PDF dl/lagarde1858_text_layer.pdf; OCR (not visually checked) p. 59 ('58-59' in Lagarde numbering), PDF p. 164; printed page number not confirmed on the scan; OCR-only
english: "Take me, O Samuel, the heifer brought to Bethlehem, in order to show the king begotten of David... For it was the first-born Word of God that descended to thee from heaven..."
page: Lagarde PDF p. 164 (printed page unconfirmed); ANF page unknown
what_it_says: A Mariological fragment calls the Word 'first-born' and says the Word descended from heaven into the womb.
limits: Transmitted through Theodoret, Dial. I (ANF note); 'first-born Word' is a hard phrase for later Nicene readers (begotten/generated tension). ANF attributes it to Hippolytus; not verified against a Theodoret manuscript.

ref: Refutation of All Heresies: title history (ANF 5 General Note, ANF lines 580-640 and 329-380 of the CCEL text)
english: ANF 5 General Note: the manuscript inscriptions read 'Refutation by Origen of all Heresies' and 'Origen's Philosophumena'; modern commentators agreed on 'Philosophumena, or the Refutation of all Heresies'; the Philosophumena was printed under Origen's name until the 1842 Athos discovery identified Hippolytus.
what_it_says: The work known as the Philosophumena is the same text as the Refutation; the Origen attribution was rejected by critics.
limits: The editorial history is from ANF's introduction, not a primary title; the Greek incipit title was not read.
